How toxins relate to each other beyond their taxonomy: which toxins look alike to a protein language model, and which molecular targets are hit independently by unrelated lineages.

A protein language model's learned embedding for every record in this dataset, reduced to 2D (UMAP). Where UniProt annotates a mature chain or peptide, that region was embedded (signal peptides and propeptides removed; multi-chain toxins as their chains joined); records with no such annotation were embedded in full. Each record’s detail panel states what was embedded. The embeddings were computed outside this page and supplied as coordinates. Fragment records (incomplete sequences) were embedded as deposited, so their positions may be less reliable. No human-assigned labels are involved: proximity reflects what the model considers similar, so toxins from unrelated lineages that land together are candidates for shared function or fold.
Top disagreements
Scroll to zoom, drag to pan. Hover a point to see what it is; click it to open that record. Choose Select (or hold Shift) and drag a box to list those toxins on the right — Shift+drag adds to the selection. Search highlights matches on the map; Enter zooms to them. CSV/FASTA export the selection (or everything if nothing is selected); SVG/PNG export the current view with its legend. Model agreement colors each toxin by how many of its 15 nearest neighbours are the same in both maps; low overlap means ProtT5 (sequence) and ProstT5 (structure-aware) disagree about what it resembles — candidates for fold-versus-sequence questions. Overlap is measured on the 2D UMAP coordinates, not the original embeddings, so some disagreement is projection noise. Tip: color by Disulfide pattern and compare ProtT5 vs ProstT5 — if same-colored points cluster in one but not the other, that's a real signal about fold (ProstT5) versus sequence (ProtT5).
Built from UniProt's own curated keywords rather than the embeddings: many venom targets are hit by toxins with completely unrelated protein folds — evolved independently, not inherited from a common ancestor. Click a target below to see which taxonomic groups and toxin classes converge on it.

Two research-oriented cuts of the data: which large well-populated protein families still have no solved 3D structure, and how confidently AlphaFold models them; and which toxins are reported as most potent. (For WHO-priority medically important snake species, see the dedicated Clinical Importance tab.)

How to read this — caveats
Values are parsed from free text that UniProt curators transcribed from the literature, so treat this as a starting point for literature review, not a validated cross-study ranking.

In vivo = LD50/PD50 from the “Toxic dose” field. Mass doses are converted to mg/kg-equivalent. Molar doses (such as nmol/g) are converted with the molecular weight of the stored mature chain and flagged “≈”, but are skipped for heterodimers and other multi-chain toxins, where one stored chain would give the wrong weight. Bounds (“>20 mg/kg”, “below 5 µg/kg”) are not treated as values. Doses in other units (µg/mL on cells, mouse units, per-insect amounts) are not parsed, so roughly 1 in 9 records that mention an LD50 are not listed here.

In vitro = IC50/EC50/Kd/Ki found in the function text, converted to nM. A list such as “IC50 of 369, 386 and 287 nM” is split into separate values, and a range keeps its lower end. Concentrations given as mass per volume (µg/mL) are not converted.

A record with several measurements is ranked by its lowest value — its best route or target, not an average. Routes, species, assay conditions and targets are not standardized across studies, and the target type tag (channel/receptor, enzyme, cell) is a keyword-based guess.

Checked: a 50-record spot check against the UniProt text (25 in vivo, 25 in vitro) found the parsed numbers correct in 48; the two errors (a “below” bound read as a value, and a heterodimer dose converted from one chain) are fixed, along with several wrong target-type tags. It is a sample, not a guarantee.

How to read this
Protein families with at least 12 characterized members. Position shows the share of members with an experimentally solved structure (PDB): families near the bottom, especially large ones at 0%, have no solved structure. Colour and the number on each card show how confident AlphaFold is about the members that are not solved: the mean pLDDT of their predicted models (>90 very high, 70–90 confident, 50–70 low, <50 very low). A family that is both unsolved and confidently modelled is where a prediction can stand in for an experiment today; an unsolved family with low confidence needs the experiment. The mean is shown only when at least 5 unsolved members have a model. pLDDT is computed over the whole translated precursor, including signal and propeptide regions.

Each dot is one protein family. Height is the share of its members that are solved; colour is AlphaFold's mean confidence for the members that are not. Click a dot for the full family.

Clinically important species — toxin-record coverage

What this shows
What this shows. The WHO Guidelines for the production, control and regulation of snake antivenom immunoglobulins (Annex 5, TRS No. 1004) list the snake species of greatest medical importance in four broad world regions — the species responsible for the most frequent or severe snakebite envenoming, and the starting point for regional antivenom-production priorities. This view cross-references that list against this dataset by organism name, so you can see, region by region, which medically important species already have a characterized Tox-Prot venom proteome and which have no characterized toxin entries at all — a real, public-health-relevant venomics gap list, distinct from the Structural Gaps view in Insights. Species are matched by binomial name only; taxonomic synonyms or recent splits may occasionally cause a miss.

Disulfide bond landscape

What this page shows
Disulfide bond positions come straight from UniProt's curated Disulfide bond feature (not predicted). Cysteines are numbered within the mature chain only where that boundary is annotated (signal peptide/propeptide cysteines are excluded, since they're cleaved off before secretion and aren't part of the final toxin). For each entry with fully-paired cysteines, bonds are re-expressed as a connectivity pattern: cysteines are numbered 1, 2, 3… in sequence order, and each bond is written as a pair of those numbers — e.g. 1-4, 2-5, 3-6 for the classic three-disulfide inhibitor cystine knot (ICK/knottin) topology. Because this numbering ignores actual sequence position, the same pattern can show up in toxins from completely unrelated animals — spiders, cone snails, scorpions — which is usually a sign of convergent evolution onto the same stable disulfide-locked scaffold, not shared ancestry. Entries with an odd cysteine count, or where the curated bonds don't fully pair every cysteine within the mature chain, are shown separately since a pattern label isn't meaningful for them. Each pattern card below also shows how often it recurs and what share of its members have a solved structure — a pattern that's both common and well-characterized structurally (like ICK/knottin) is generally a safer bet as a drug-design scaffold than a rare, structurally unexplored one. You can also color the Embedding Map (Toxin Relationships) and the Taxonomy tree by disulfide pattern to see whether a scaffold clusters by sequence, by lineage, or both.

Most common connectivity patterns

Each card is one complete pattern: how all the cysteines of a toxin are paired, numbered in order along the mature chain. For example 1-4, 2-5, 3-6 means the 1st cysteine bonds to the 4th, the 2nd to the 5th and the 3rd to the 6th. The number on the card is how many toxins share that exact pattern.

Unpaired cysteine outliers

Entries where the curated disulfide bonds leave one or more cysteines unmatched — sometimes a free catalytic/reactive thiol, sometimes an intermolecular (inter-chain) bond to a different protein, occasionally just a curation gap. Worth a manual look before relying on these for framework classification.

How to read this
Built from NCBI's classification for each source organism, domain down to species. Use it to see how toxin coverage, structural data, and disulfide scaffolds are distributed across the animal kingdom — including cases where unrelated lineages (say, a spider and a cone snail) independently evolved the same disulfide scaffold. Long runs of single-child ancestry are compressed into one row, shown as a breadcrumb, so you're not scrolling through a dozen nested clades with nothing else branching off them.

About this atlas

The Tox-Prot programme
where this data comes from

The underlying records come from Tox-Prot, UniProt's animal toxin annotation programme, which systematically curates proteins secreted in animal venom. Venomous contributors include snakes, spiders, scorpions, cone snails, centipedes, jellyfish, insects, sea anemones, lizards, a handful of fish, and platypuses — and the programme also covers toxins from poisonous animals that have no venom-delivery apparatus at all, such as certain mammals, toads and ticks.

Every entry meets the same quality bar as the rest of UniProtKB/Swiss-Prot, with particular attention paid to what's actually known about a toxin's function and mechanism of action, its post-translational modifications, and its 3D structure — all unusually well documented in this corner of biology compared with most protein families.

Toxins tend to be short and heavily post-translationally modified, so they're most often characterized directly at the protein level rather than purely inferred from sequence — part of why this dataset carries so much detailed, hands-on annotation.

What this tool adds
on top of the raw UniProt export

This atlas indexes an export of 8,274 reviewed Tox-Prot records (taxonomy: Metazoa, filtered to entries carrying a tissue-specificity annotation): protein and gene names, organism, function, tissue specificity, PTMs, subcellular location, keywords, protein family, cross-references to PDB structures and literature, and sequence — laid out for browsing, filtering, comparison and export rather than one entry at a time.

Taxonomic category (snake, spider, scorpion, etc.) is assigned from each record's NCBI taxonomic lineage (for example, anything under Serpentes is a snake). The broader "toxin class" grouping (3FTx, SVMP, PLA2, disintegrin…) is inferred from the protein family and name strings. Both are conveniences for browsing — they are not UniProt fields — and the toxin class in particular may occasionally misclassify an entry.

WHO medically important species overlay
a second data source, layered on top

Entries whose organism matches a species on the list of medically important venomous snakes in the WHO Guidelines for the production, control and regulation of snake antivenom immunoglobulins (Annex 5, TRS No. 1004, Tables A5.3–A5.6) are flagged with a WHO badge, filterable in Browse and broken down region by region in the dedicated Clinical Importance tab. That list is WHO's own starting point for regional antivenom-production priorities, not a Tox-Prot annotation — species are matched here by binomial organism name only.

This lets the same dataset answer a different kind of question than the Structural Gaps view in Insights: not "which protein families lack a solved structure", but "which snakes that actually cause the most snakebite morbidity and mortality worldwide already have — or still lack — any characterized toxin sequence at all."

InterPro domain/family signatures
from UniProt's own InterPro cross-references

5,908 of 8,274 records (71%) carry one or more InterPro entries — pulled straight from UniProt's own InterPro cross-reference column for this record set, not a separate InterPro query, so accession matching is exact. InterPro entries are authoritative, sequence-signature-based classifications (domain / family / homologous superfamily / repeat) and often catch entries that UniProt's free-text "Protein family" field leaves unclassified.

Shown as an "InterPro entry" filter in Browse, as linked chips on each record's detail card, and as a "Top InterPro entries" chart in Stats. Entries are displayed by accession (e.g. IPR001762) with a link straight to the InterPro entry page — this tool doesn't bundle InterPro's entry names/descriptions locally, so the name and a fuller description are one click away rather than shown inline.

Sequence, processing and evidence annotations
all taken from UniProt features, not predicted

Each record's detail panel shows the full translated precursor sequence, with the signal peptide, propeptide and mature chain marked on a sequence map and in a cleavage note, so you can design constructs from the whole precursor while seeing which part is actually secreted. It also shows curated disulfide bonds, modified residues and glycosylation, observed mass (where UniProt has one, compared against the computed mass), the UniProt protein-existence level, and a flag for fragment entries whose sequence is incomplete.

Physicochemical properties (pI, charge, instability, GRAVY and so on) are computed in your browser from the stored sequence with standard ProtParam-style formulas; they do not account for cleavage or PTMs.

Views built on top of the records
what each tab adds

Organism lists every source species with its toxin classes; Taxonomy arranges the organisms in the NCBI lineage tree; Disulfides summarizes bond counts and connectivity patterns (cysteines numbered within the mature chain); Clinical Importance overlays the WHO list of medically important snakes; Toxin Relationships holds the embedding map and the keyword-based shared-target view; Insights covers reported potency and structural gaps; Similarity Search runs a local Smith-Waterman alignment against all records.

Mechanism of action terms are the Gene Ontology molecular-function annotations UniProt attaches to each record, grouped for browsing.

Embedding maps
ProtT5 and ProstT5, projected with UMAP

The two maps in Toxin Relationships come from protein language model embeddings (ProtT5 for sequence, ProstT5 as a structure-aware model) of each record's mature chain or peptide region where UniProt annotates one (otherwise the full sequence), reduced to two dimensions with UMAP (umap-learn with default settings: n_neighbors = 15, min_dist = 0.1, Euclidean metric; 2 components; random_state = 42), separately for each model. Embeddings were generated with the ProtSpace embedding notebook (Rostlab/prot_t5_xl_half_uniref50-enc for ProtT5 and Rostlab/ProstT5_fp16 for ProstT5, one mean-pooled vector per protein). They were computed outside this page; the page only displays the coordinates. Distances and cluster shapes in a UMAP are not quantitative, axes are arbitrary, and different runs give different layouts.

“Nearest neighbours” and the “Model agreement” view are measured on these 2D coordinates, so they are approximate: some disagreement between the two models is projection noise, not biology.

Values worked out by this tool
derived here, so check before relying on them

Animal group (assigned from the NCBI lineage), toxin class (inferred from family and protein names), disulfide connectivity patterns, mechanism groupings, potency and lethality values (parsed from UniProt free text, with the limits described in Insights), computed physicochemical properties, and the embedding neighbours and agreement scores. None of these are original UniProt fields.

How to cite
the atlas, its data, and the methods behind it

If this atlas helps your work, please cite the underlying resources — UniProt and the Tox-Prot programme first and foremost — and mention the atlas itself:

Venom Atlas (2026). An interactive browser for UniProtKB/Swiss-Prot Tox-Prot animal toxin records. Data: UniProt Tox-Prot export, retrieved September 2026.

UniProt data are released under CC BY 4.0. Embedding coordinates, derived values (animal group, toxin class, disulfide patterns, potency parsing, neighbour scores) were produced for this atlas and are not UniProt fields.
